revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Total operating revenue: government-funded aged-care bed-day fees (rest home, hospital, dementia and psychogeriatric care), accommodation supplements, resident-funded premium services, and adjacent revenue (Cibus catering, Home Support, Radius Shop, Luma).

For Radius: ~87% of revenue is the government-set bed-day rate paid by Health New Zealand, WINZ and ACC, so Radius is fundamentally a price-taker on volume (occupancy, bed count) rather than price. FY2026 revenue grew 14% to $205.5m on 94.9% average occupancy (+2.1pp) plus the St Allisa and Karori bolt-on acquisitions.

What to watch:

  • Whether the August 2026 Ministerial Advisory Group's recommended ~7.1% bed-day price uplift is actually legislated and funded in a future Budget -- it is the single biggest lever on this line and is NOT yet enacted policy
  • Occupancy trending toward management's 97-98% aspiration versus the harder-to-sustain admission/discharge churn of a higher-acuity bed mix
  • New-build and bolt-on bed additions (Karori settled May 2026, ~20 new 80-100 bed homes targeted over the coming years)

ebitdaNi.title: EBITDA & Net Income
ebitdaNi.content:
EBITDA (earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization) versus net income attributable to shareholders.

For Radius: FY2026 EBITDA of $39.1m and net income of $10.1m both grew faster than revenue as occupancy recovered and cost discipline held, but the gap between the two lines is unusually wide for this company because of the large interest and depreciation load from ~$213m of combined bank debt and IFRS-16 lease liabilities sitting between EBITDA and net income.

What to watch:

  • FY2019/FY2020 figures are from OCR-extracted scanned filings (lower confidence) and FY2020 is the IFRS-16 adoption year, which reshapes depreciation and finance costs below the EBITDA line -- read pre/post FY2020 EBITDA as broadly comparable but net income as not
  • Whether wage inflation (employee costs +16% in FY2026) continues to outpace revenue growth and compress the EBITDA-to-net-income conversion

margins.title: EBITDA Margin & Net Margin
margins.content:
EBITDA and net income each as a percentage of revenue.

For Radius: EBITDA margin has been rebuilding from a FY2024 trough (~16.8%) back toward ~19-20% as occupancy recovered and higher-acuity, better-funded beds grew as a share of the mix; the DCF base case models a further gradual drift to 20.5% by Year 10. Net margin is structurally much thinner (4-5%) because of the heavy interest and lease-interest load below EBITDA.

What to watch:

  • Whether the government-set bed-day rate keeps pace with minimum-wage increases (to NZ$23.95/hr from April 2026) and general wage inflation -- Radius is a price-taker on the revenue side but not on the cost side
  • The DCF's bear case models margin compressing back to ~16% (roughly the FY2024 level) if funding freezes while costs keep rising

leverage.title: Total Debt vs Shareholders' Equity
leverage.content:
Total debt (bank borrowings plus IFRS-16 lease liabilities) against shareholders' equity.

For Radius: this is the single most important chart for understanding the business. Roughly half of the 25 care homes are leased rather than owned, so total debt of $213.1m at FY2026 splits into $71.6m of bank borrowings and $141.5m of IFRS-16 lease liabilities -- against only $76.3m of shareholders' equity. The 'capital-light' growth model (new beds funded and owned by third-party property investors, then leased back to Radius) keeps the balance sheet smaller than an integrated owner-developer like Summerset or Ryman, but it trades that off for a large, growing lease obligation. Management's own target is Net Bank Debt/EBITDA below 2.5x (bank debt only); FY2026 net bank debt was $68.7m, up just 1% YoY.

What to watch:

  • FY2020 shows lease liabilities jumping from $0 to $185m -- this is the IFRS-16 accounting adoption creating a balance-sheet liability for existing leases, not a real one-year quadrupling of obligations
  • Bank covenant compliance (quarterly-tested fixed charge cover, leverage and equity ratio) -- currently met with a clean, unqualified FY2026 audit opinion, but headroom is worth monitoring given equity of only $76m against $213m of combined obligations
  • The DCF deliberately excludes lease liabilities from its own net-debt figure and instead charges the full lease cash cost (principal + interest) inside the projected cash flows, to avoid double-counting roughly half the enterprise as both a liability and an operating cost

fcf.title: Reported FCF vs Owner FCF (DCF basis)
fcf.content:
Reported FreeCashFlow in the CSV is operating cash flow less capital expenditure, as filed. It is NOT the same as the DCF's owner FCF.

For Radius: reported FCF excludes IFRS-16 lease principal repayments (which sit in the financing section of the cash flow statement, not operating) and Radius additionally reports both bank interest AND lease interest inside operating cash flow. The DCF's owner-FCF bridge starts from reported FCF, adds back bank interest paid (since the DCF's own net-debt bridge charges bank debt separately and would otherwise double-count it), then deducts lease principal, SBC and interest income -- lease interest stays deducted exactly once, where it already sits inside reported OCF. The result: FY2026 reported FCF of $9.05m becomes owner FCF of $10.34m, the true unlevered cash generation before financing choices.

What to watch:

  • Do not use reported FreeCashFlow alone to judge cash generation for this company -- it is a distorted mix of levered and unlevered items
  • The Owner FCF history spans two large negative years (FY2022 -$31.5m, FY2023 -$50.9m) driven by acquisition-heavy capex, not operating deterioration -- shown here for audit, not as a trend to extrapolate

ocfCapex.title: Operating Cash Flow vs CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Cash generated from operations before capital expenditure, versus capital expenditure spent in the period.

For Radius: FY2022 ($38.8m) and FY2023 ($58.7m) capex spikes were acquisition-heavy facility purchases, not maintenance spend -- normalized maintenance-plus-modest-development capex has more recently run 2.4-3.5% of revenue. FY2026's $16.1m (7.8% of revenue) was driven by the St Allisa business acquisition, largely recycled via a sale-and-leaseback to a related party, consistent with the capital-light growth model where new beds are typically funded by third-party property investors rather than Radius's own balance sheet.

What to watch:

  • OCF comfortably covers normalized maintenance capex; the wide OCF-capex gap in most years reflects the capital-light model shifting growth capex off Radius's own books and into third-party-funded leases (captured in the lease cost line, not here)

equity.title: Shareholders' Equity
equity.content:
Total shareholders' equity (net assets) at each period end.

For Radius: equity has grown from $17.9m (FY2019) to $76.3m (FY2026), but not smoothly: the FY2022 jump from $24.1m to $70.1m was a capital raise, and FY2023/FY2024 both show impairment-driven net losses that shrank equity growth. Because of this, the DCF explicitly avoids using equity CAGR as a valuation growth anchor, using revenue CAGR (10.3% over 5 years) instead.

What to watch:

  • Equity of $76.3m against $213.1m of combined bank and lease obligations is thin -- book value here is not a reliable floor on downside
  • FY2020's asset base (and by extension book composition) shifted materially on IFRS-16 adoption -- read equity trend cleanly from FY2021 onward

cash.title: Cash & Equivalents
cash.content:
Cash and cash equivalents held at each period end.

For Radius: Radius runs a lean cash balance ($2.6-4.2m across most periods, briefly as low as $0.5m in FY2023) rather than holding a cash cushion, consistent with a leveraged, bank-facility-funded growth model -- excess cash is used to pay down the ASB facility or fund development rather than accumulate on the balance sheet.

What to watch:

  • Cash levels are only meaningful alongside undrawn ASB facility headroom (not shown here), since Radius manages liquidity through committed bank lines rather than a cash buffer

sharesDividend.title: Shares Outstanding & Dividend per Share
sharesDividend.content:
Total ordinary shares on issue and the total dividend declared per share for the fiscal year.

For Radius: a 14:1 share split took effect 8 December 2020. FY2019 and FY2020 carry the pre-split raw count of 12.5m shares; FY2021 onward is post-split (175m rising to 283.9m via the FY2022 capital raise and subsequent LTIP issuance). The FY2020-to-FY2021 jump on this chart is the split, not a capital raise or dilution event. Dividends were introduced after listing and the final FY2026 dividend was raised 50% to 1.20 cents per share (fully imputed), for a FY2026 total of 2.2 cps and an approximate 8.0% gross yield at the FY26 close.

What to watch:

  • Never compare FY2019/FY2020 raw share counts or per-share figures directly against FY2021+ without applying the 14:1 adjustment
  • The dividend policy targets 40-70% of AFFO; FY2026's actual payout was 49% of AFFO, leaving room for further increases if AFFO keeps growing
